body.text: The 28 November polls are being fought largely on bread-and-butter concerns, but China-linked controversies and the proposed hiring of Indian workers have given them a wider significance

On 28 November 2026, Taiwan is scheduled to hold its next round of nine-in-one local elections, in which voters will choose representatives across multiple tiers of local government. Unlike presidential elections, which are often dominated by questions of national identity, cross-strait relations, and Taiwan's international positioning, the local polls are expected to focus on issues that directly affect citizens' everyday lives. Issues such as rising living costs, school meals, tainted cooking oil—which triggered a major protest by supporters of the Kuomintang (KMT), who blamed the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) for failing to take harsh measures against the culprits—and how to develop large parcels of urban land have all become part of the broader political debate. These concerns show how closely local electoral competition in Taiwan is tied to voters' immediate socioeconomic interests. The author's observation of the KMT-organised protest rally over food safety further demonstrates how everyday governance issues can become instruments of political mobilisation and electoral competition.

The distinctive characteristic of Taiwan’s local elections is the prominence of local issues. Voters are more likely to assess candidates based on their proposed solutions to local problems, economic pressures, and public services. In presidential elections, by contrast, the debate revolves around how Taiwan manages—and should manage—its relationship with China, safeguards its sovereignty, and navigates its international relations.

The principal contenders are the KMT, the oldest party, widely known as the Blue Camp; the DPP, known as the Green Camp; and the Taiwan People's Party (TPP), also called the White Camp, a third alternative once seen as a potential kingmaker.

Taipei has traditionally leaned towards the Blue Camp, led by the KMT, though the city's political landscape has shifted over the years. Dr Ko Wen-je, founder of the TPP, served as Taipei's mayor from 2014-22. He first won the mayoralty as an independent and went on to found the TPP in 2019. In 2024, he contested the presidential election but lost, securing only 26.46 percent of the vote.
Ko's political career later became mired in a corruption scandal, which led to his arrest and a 17-year prison sentence. Since then, the TPP has struggled to retain its appeal among voters.

The Taipei mayoral race is arguably among the most closely watched contests in Taiwan, not only because Taipei is the capital, but also because of the historical link between the mayor's office and national leadership. Since Taiwan's democratisation and the introduction of direct mayoral elections in 1994, two former Taipei mayors have gone on to become president, the country's highest office. The table below lists the former Taipei mayors who became president of Taiwan.
Note: Lee Teng-hui served as Taipei's mayor before direct mayoral elections were introduced in 1994, when the post was filled by appointment.

In the current election cycle, Taipei is witnessing a competitive six-way mayoral race, with the contest centred on two leading candidates: incumbent Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the KMT and Shen Pao-yang, also known as Puma Shen, of the DPP.

In a televised debate to which only the two frontrunners were invited, Chiang largely highlighted the projects completed under his administration. These included key infrastructure works, efforts to attract major investment (among them Nvidia's plan to establish its first overseas headquarters in Taipei), and improvements to the city's school meal programmes. Shen's campaign, in contrast, has focused on urban afforestation, tackling child abuse, and improving the nutritional quality of school meals.

Given Taipei's historical association with the Blue Camp, the growing support base for Shen has drawn considerable attention. Several opinion polls indicate that he is gaining ground and emerging as a serious challenger to the incumbent. This suggests that the Taipei mayoral contest could become an important test of shifting electoral dynamics in a city long associated with the KMT.

It is difficult to discuss Taiwan's elections, whether local or national, without addressing the role of China. Despite the emphasis on local governance and everyday socioeconomic concerns, cross-strait relations continue to find their way into the electoral discourse. This is particularly evident in two emerging concerns: the participation of Chinese spouses (Chinese citizens married to Taiwanese citizens) in local elections, and allegations of Chinese interference in Taiwan's electoral process.

According to Central Election Commission Chairperson You Ying-lung, 26 Chinese spouses are seeking to contest various positions in the 2026 elections: 19 village and borough chief posts, along with seven other elected offices. Under Taiwan's legal framework, Chinese spouses seeking public office must meet specific requirements concerning their citizenship and their household registration status in mainland China.

One such case involves Li Chen-hsiu of the TPP, a China-born woman married to a Taiwanese national, who was disqualified from contesting the Zhubei mayoral election in Hsinchu County. The Hsinchu County Election Commission cited Article 21 of the Cross-Strait Act, which stipulates a ten-year household registration requirement for naturalised Chinese spouses seeking certain public offices. According to Li, she acquired Republic of China (ROC) citizenship in 1999. However, she did not submit documentary proof to the relevant immigration authorities confirming that she had relinquished her household registration in mainland China until March 2025.

Another significant concern relates to allegations that Beijing is attempting to influence Taiwan's local elections through organised voter mobilisation and financial support. According to National Security Bureau (NSB) Director-General Tsai Ming-yen, China is mobilising airlines to offer discounted tickets to selected Taiwanese citizens living in China so that they can return home to vote in the November elections. These voters are guided to back the candidates Beijing favours. Beyond voter mobilisation, concerns have also been raised over alleged illicit funding directed towards political candidates and organisations in Taiwan. Such allegations, if proved, would raise serious questions about foreign interference in Taiwan's elections.

Lin Te-wang, founder and chairman of the Taiwan People's Communist Party, was detained in November 2026 on suspicion of accepting instructions and financial support from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to contest the upcoming local elections. According to Taiwanese prosecutors, Lin received funding and instructions from Beijing to run for the position of borough chief in Tainan, a city in southern Taiwan.

Another incident that drew national attention involved Taiwanese comedian Huang Yi-hao, who was allegedly targeted in a staged traffic accident by individuals acting on instructions from a person in mainland China. Huang, known for satirical performances criticising Chinese President Xi Jinping and the CCP, was struck by a car while riding his scooter in September 2026. Taiwanese prosecutors indicted five individuals in connection with the incident, which has raised concerns that cross-border intimidation is being used to silence critics of the Chinese government, even within Taiwan.

In November 2026, independent lawmaker Kao Chin Su-mei and three of her associates were indicted on national security and corruption charges. According to prosecutors, individuals associated with her received more than US$5.17 million in Chinese funding between 2005 and 2016 for various projects and organisational activities in Taiwan. Prosecutors further alleged that Chinese officials had issued instructions concerning political activities, election campaigns, and legislative matters.

Taken together, these incidents show how far China-related concerns have become intertwined with Taiwan's domestic electoral politics. From alleged financial support to political candidates and voter mobilisation to the intimidation of public figures critical of Beijing, these cases highlight the different ways in which, according to Taiwan's authorities, external influence may operate within the domestic political environment.

Taiwan's domestic elections have traditionally focused on local governance and everyday concerns, with relatively limited emphasis on external affairs. Ahead of the 2026 elections, however, the issue of migrant workers and their integration into Taiwanese society has emerged as an important subject of public debate. In particular, the proposed entry of Indian migrant workers into Taiwan has attracted considerable attention and, at times, generated controversy.

Since April 2026, several debates and discussions have taken place over the potential recruitment of Indian workers. In May 2026, independent candidate Lee Hung-yi, contesting in Kaohsiung, faced criticism over a campaign poster opposing the recruitment of Indian migrant workers. The controversy highlighted the political sensitivities surrounding the proposed labour agreement between India and Taiwan. Under an earlier understanding, the two sides had agreed to facilitate the recruitment of 1,000 Indian workers for Taiwan's manufacturing, agricultural, and caregiving sectors. These industries face considerable labour shortages, partly because of Taiwan's declining birth rate and shrinking working-age population. Public opposition to the proposed programme has, however, put its implementation on hold.

Taiwan relies heavily on foreign workers across several sectors of its economy. In November 2026, it signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Philippines for hiring Filipino workers under the Special Hiring Program in Taiwan (SHPT), aiming to facilitate direct recruitment in the hospitality sector. The initiative builds on the substantial Filipino workforce already in Taiwan, which numbers more than 200,000.
There is little doubt that the recruitment of Indian labour will remain part of Taiwan's domestic political discourse, and it may well return to the debate ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

This development offers an important point of consideration for India. New Delhi could explore a revised recruitment framework with Taipei, drawing lessons from Taiwan's direct-hiring arrangements with the Philippines. It could also consider initiating a fresh round of discussions with Taiwan after the local elections conclude on 28 November, which would allow both Taiwanese employers' and Indian workers' interests to be addressed. There is little doubt that the recruitment of Indian labour will remain part of Taiwan's domestic political discourse, and it may well return to the debate ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Looking ahead, President Lai Ching-te may seek a second term, while the KMT will look to identify a candidate to challenge him; at present, indications are that Chiang Wan-an is being considered. The debate over Indian migrant workers could therefore extend beyond labour shortages to broader questions about Taiwan's approach to foreign workers, immigration policy, and economic cooperation with India.

Dr. Manoj Kumar Panigrahi is an Assistant Professor and Director of the Centre for Northeast Asian Studies at the Jindal School of International Affairs, O.P. Jindal Global University. He teaches courses on Taiwan's history and politics and on cross-strait relations.
